title-group.article-title: Preclinical Evaluation of Human Donor-Derived Micronized Bone Marrow Stroma/Parenchyma Versus Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate in a Rat Model of Post-Traumatic Knee Osteoarthritis

contrib-group.aff: 1The Steadman Philippon Research Institute, Vail, CO 81657, USA

license.license-p: This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License.

abstract.p: Bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) is widely used as a source of mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs); however, BMAC lacks essential bone marrow extracellular matrix (ECM) components. At 4 weeks after treatment, BMAC significantly increased the paw withdrawal threshold compared with PBS (p = 0.0068), whereas BMAX™ significantly reduced knee joint swelling compared with both PBS (p = 0.0235) and BMAC (p = 0.0039). Flow cytometry identified CD73+ CD90+/CD105+/CD45− populations. Cells were cultured at 37 °C in 5% CO2.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are multipotent progenitor cells capable of differentiating into adipocytes, osteoblasts, and chondrocytes. Bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) has gained popularity as an autologous MSC source for a wide range of regenerative medicine applications, including knee osteoarthritis (OA) [1,2,3].

However, MSCs are inherently rare in bone marrow aspirate, comprising approximately 0.001% to 0.01% of total nucleated cells [13,14]. Whether this tissue-preserving approach yields greater therapeutic efficacy in vivo has not been directly tested.

sec.title: 2.1. Human Bone Marrow Collection and Preparation
sec.p: Bone marrow subcortical bone cores and aspirate were obtained from a single consented 50-year-old female donor (BMI 19.5). Aspirate was anticoagulated with preservative-free heparin at a final concentration of 10 U/mL.

sec.title: 2.2. Flow Cytometry
sec.p: MSCs were identified via flow cytometry following the ISCT minimal criteria [21] as previously described: CD34−, CD45−, CD73+, CD90+, CD105+. See Figure 2 for the gating strategy. Full protocols are available at the study repository.

sec.title: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Results are presented as mean ± SD. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The effect size was computed as d = (\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma for the primary comparison.

sec.title: 3.1. BMAX Cells Favor Pericyte Expansion During Culture
sec.p: We found adhering cells from BMAX formed more colonies in 14 days (Figure 2A,B). The percentage of CD146+CD45− cells increased over passages and significantly increased at P2 compared to BMAC-derived adhering cells (p = 0.0446).

caption.p: Characterization of micronized bone marrow cells. (A,B) Representative CFU-F assay images. Significant difference: * p < 0.05. ns: not significant.

sec.title: 3.2. Improved Pain-Related Behaviors After DMM Surgery
sec.p: In the knee-bend assay, BMAX™ significantly reduced movement-evoked pain versus PBS at both 4 and 8 weeks post-injection (p = 0.0011 and p = 0.0027), as did BMAC at 8 weeks (p = 0.0255) (Table 2, Figure 4B).

fn.p: Data are presented as mean ± SD.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: BMAC is widely used to deliver MSCs to affected tissues with positive clinical outcomes [30,31]. Capturing this bone-associated MSC population may contribute to the greater adherence observed here.

This study did have limitations. First, the number of animals was relatively small, which may have limited the statistical power to detect differences for some outcome measures. Second, both preparations were derived from a single human donor, so the generalizability of our findings remains to be established.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study demonstrates that retention of native extracellular matrix within a micronized bone marrow preparation enhances the therapeutic potential of bone marrow-derived cell therapy in a preclinical OA model.
